description: Drama Years 9-10 width tiers — ACARA v9. All strands are capability strands; primary axis is task_contexts.
subject: Drama

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the command term at Y9-10. Minimum involves meeting the command term in one task context — one devised or scripted piece, one analytical investigation, one performance with evaluation.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope from elaborations — the range of tasks, conventions, styles and analytical contexts a well-taught Y9-10 class would engage with across a unit.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment adding new conventions, styles, cultural traditions, collaborative contexts or analytical frameworks — not harder versions of the same task.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are the primary source. First Nations elaborations for E02 appear in wider; others include First Nations directions where indicated.

AC9ADR10C01.minimum_width: Student devises or interprets drama with a clear stated intention (audience, purpose, style/form) using at least three deliberate element or convention choices, and can explain each.
AC9ADR10C01.typical_width: Students use frameworks (stimulus material, character lists, narrative outlines) to devise drama; they consider audience, viewpoint, purpose and form; they manipulate language, movement and symbol to convey tensions; they employ multiple conventions; they collaborate to combine scenes through play-building.
wider: Students develop non-linear drama presenting the same story from multiple character perspectives, using narrator/chorus or disruptive character conventions
Students script scenes developed through improvisation, applying play-building techniques to create a cohesive scripted work
Students devise drama in response to an issue from another learning area, building purposeful cross-disciplinary work
Students investigate conventions from Asian, African or other non-Western dramatic traditions and apply one in their own devising, reflecting on its cultural significance
elaborations: using a teacher-provided framework to develop drama collaboratively
considering contexts such as audiences, viewpoints, intentions and style/form when planning interpretations
conveying tensions through manipulation of language, movement and symbol
devising drama presenting a range of perspectives using non-linear structures
scripting scenes from improvisation using play-building techniques
using props, set items or digital tools to enhance communication of meaning

AC9ADR10C02.minimum_width: Student identifies at least three aesthetic choices in their drama, explains how each contributes to unified meaning, and documents at least two refinements made during rehearsal.
AC9ADR10C02.typical_width: Students evaluate how ideas, emotions and audience response inform refinement; they manipulate pace, cues, vocal tone, proximity and transitions; they collaborate as directors and performers; they consider design elements (costume, set, lighting, sound); they manipulate actor-audience relationships.
wider: Students take on specific production roles (director, designer, stage manager) and articulate aesthetic decisions from within that role
Students collaborate with community members in a shared production process, managing collective ownership of aesthetic choices
Students document and analyse their refinement process using annotated scripts, rehearsal notes or video review
elaborations: evaluating how ideas, emotions and audience response inform refinement
reflecting on how successfully intentions, meaning and effects were achieved and what can be learnt for future practice
strengthening dramatic action by manipulating pace, cues, vocal tone, proximity and transitions
collaborating as director — blocking and staging to communicate intended meaning
taking on roles such as stage manager, sound/lighting designer, costumes, writer, director
considering the impact of design elements on meaning and aesthetic effect
manipulating elements and conventions to create and manipulate actor-audience relationships

AC9ADR10D01.minimum_width: Student identifies at least two physical and two psychological dimensions of a character through analysis, and demonstrates at least one performance choice grounded in psychological analysis.
AC9ADR10D01.typical_width: Students use text analysis to explore implied and underlying aspects of character; they refine vocal skills through character-focused warm-ups; they experiment with, reflect on and refine styles and conventions; they workshop comedy forms, physical theatre or non-realistic conventions.
wider: Students perform the same character through two different stylistic conventions, reflecting on how style shapes character expression
Students develop a character communicating both individual psychology and collective/cultural identity simultaneously
Students explore historical or non-Western performance styles (Commedia, Noh, Brechtian) and develop skills within one, applying insights to their devised or scripted work
elaborations: experimenting with, reflecting on and refining styles and conventions to shape action
using text analysis to inform exploring and refining implied aspects of character
refining vocal skills through warm-ups focusing on character and delivery or movement

AC9ADR10D02.minimum_width: Student produces an analysis-level reflection on at least two specific dramatic choices (element, convention, or approach), and documents at least one change to practice motivated by that analysis.
AC9ADR10D02.typical_width: Students compare use of conventions across performance styles; they analyse element and convention choices to affect meaning; they shape their use of elements and conventions to achieve intended meaning; they evaluate how successfully intentions and effects were achieved.
wider: Students maintain a reflective practice journal across a substantial project, analysing how their thinking evolved across multiple iterations
Students engage in peer-critique sessions using a shared analytical framework, developing capacity for giving and receiving high-quality developmental feedback
Students use video review of their rehearsals to analyse the gap between intended and enacted choices, documenting specific refinements in response
elaborations: comparing use of conventions to explore and challenge power and oppression across performance styles
analysing and making choices about manipulating elements and experimenting with conventions (subtext, beats) to affect meaning
shaping use of elements, conventions and styles to achieve intended meaning or effect

AC9ADR10E01.minimum_width: Student identifies at least one drama that challenges a perspective or meaning, names at least one dramatic device used to create that challenge, and analyses at least two examples from different cultural or historical contexts.
AC9ADR10E01.typical_width: Students view diverse styles/forms — historical and modern, Australian and Asian, realist and non-realist — to understand how conventions communicate and challenge; they consider social context, cultural movements, historical influences and actor-audience relationships; they identify how contemporary performance styles affect meaning.
wider: Students investigate drama that uses Brechtian distancing, satire or irony to challenge ideas, comparing its operation to drama that creates empathy and identification
Students investigate drama from a country or region in Asia, considering the social, cultural and historical context in which it challenges or affirms dominant meanings
Students investigate a contemporary global drama phenomenon (immersive theatre, mediatisation, site-specific performance) and analyse how it reframes audience relationship
elaborations: viewing a performance and considering how elements use symbol or movement to make meaning
investigating ways drama texts are created and developed collaboratively
viewing examples of varied styles within a style to understand shared and differing conventions
using Viewpoints to ask questions about social context, cultural movements and historical influences
viewing historical texts where artists use contemporary performance conventions to affect meaning

AC9ADR10E02.minimum_width: Student identifies both a celebration and a challenge of Australian identity in a specific First Nations drama work, naming the dramatic elements involved.
AC9ADR10E02.typical_width: Students investigate how and why practitioners collaborate with communities to present contemporary First Nations theatre; they consider global influences on First Nations drama; they investigate how contemporary First Nations theatre explores and challenges histories and Australian identity; they compare and critique drama celebrating and challenging Australian identity.
wider: Students investigate how a First Nations drama work navigates the tension between international festival audiences and local community audiences
Students investigate the relationship between specific First Nations drama works and legal or political history (land rights, sovereignty, recognition)
Students compare how First Nations and non-Indigenous Australian dramatists treat the same historical or contemporary issues, examining whose version of Australian identity is foregrounded
elaborations: investigating how and why drama practitioners work collaboratively with communities to present contemporary First Nations theatre
considering how global trends in drama influence First Nations drama
investigating how Contemporary First Nations Australian Theatre explores and challenges histories of Australia and Australian identity
comparing and critiquing ways contemporary drama celebrates and challenges influences on Australia's identity

AC9ADR10P01.minimum_width: Student sustains performance intention — character, voice, physicality — across a complete piece, and produces an evaluation addressing intention, execution and audience effect.
AC9ADR10P01.typical_width: Students convey tensions through voice, movement and symbol; they engage audiences and elicit responses; they perform in sustained class or stage contexts; they adhere to protocols for collective ownership; they evaluate how successfully intentions and effects were achieved.
wider: Students perform devised drama created with community members, observing protocols for collective ownership and cultural authority
Students perform in an extended context (multi-scene, festival, community presentation) requiring sustained stamina and consistency
Students compare their own performance evaluation with collected audience feedback, analysing the gap between intended and experienced meaning
elaborations: conveying tensions in stories, characters, relationships through voice, movement and symbol to engage audiences
presenting and performing devised or scripted drama created in a shared process with community members, adhering to collective ownership protocols
performing on stage or in class in a sustained presentation
reflecting on and evaluating how successfully intentions, meaning and effects were achieved, and what can be learnt for future practice
